To name the parts of the body.
To say what hurts: mă doare capul, mă dor picioarele.
To describe symptoms to the doctor and understand the advice.
To talk about the future with “o să” + subjunctive (and recognise “voi + infinitive”).
To review the A1 level: a fi, a avea, the article, genders, the present, the subjunctive, the imperative, the compound perfect.
On Tuesday, after the trip, Nora wakes up with a temperature and a red throat. Mrs Pop sends her straight to her daughter Ioana, who is a family doctor at a surgery in the neighbourhood.
Hello, Nora! My mother told me you’re ill. Have a seat, please. What’s hurting?
Hello! My throat hurts and my head hurts. And all my bones ache.
How long have you had these symptoms?
Since yesterday evening. Last night I had a temperature: thirty-eight point five.
Do you have a cough too?
A little. Especially in the morning.
Open your mouth, please. Say “aaa”… Yes, your throat is very red. Now breathe in deeply… Your lungs are fine. It’s a cold, nothing serious.
Thank goodness! Do I need antibiotics?
No, there’s no need. I’ll write you a prescription: a cough syrup and tablets for the fever. Take one tablet every eight hours if your temperature is over thirty-eight degrees.
Can I go to the office tomorrow?
No. You’re going to stay at home for three days. Drink lots of fluids, tea with honey and lemon, and rest. And don’t go out without a hat!
That’s what your mother told me too.
Mum is always right. Oh, and one more thing… Radu called me this morning. He has a temperature too. It looks like a “team” cold.
Oh… I’m sorry. It’s my fault, I gave him the scarf too late.
It’s nobody’s fault. But I think my son will thank you for the scarf himself. Get well soon, Nora!
to hurt: “mă doare” = it hurts me
to go out: tu ieși (you go out)
“m-a sunat” = called me on the phone (past)
to believe, to think: eu cred (I think)
The stress falls on “doa-”: mă DOA-re. “oa” is pronounced as one syllable.
Watch the diacritics: “gât”, “mână”, “însănătoșire”. Without them, many words are no longer correct.
“o să” is pronounced together and quickly: “osă merg”. In very fast speech you even hear “o-să-mrg”.
For parts of the body, Romanian usually uses the article, not the possessive: “Mă doare capul” (not “capul meu”), “Mă spăl pe mâini” (I wash my hands).
“A durea” (to hurt) works like “a plăcea”: the body part that hurts is the subject, and the person is in the accusative (mă, te, îl, o…). The verb agrees with the body part.
After the trip our legs ache.
You don’t say “am durere la cap” but “mă doare capul”. And: “îl doare” (him) / “o doare” (her).
3. At the doctor’s and at the pharmacy
I have a temperature / a cough / a cold.
How long have you had the symptoms?
Take one tablet three times a day.
Do you have anything for a headache? (at the pharmacy)
In an emergency in Romania, call 112. Ambulance, police and fire brigade share the same number.
When someone is ill, you wish them: “Însănătoșire grabnică!” or, more simply, “Să te faci bine!” (Get better!).
In everyday speech, the future is most often formed with “o să” + the subjunctive form (the one used after “să”). The “o” never changes.
You’re going to stay at home for three days.
I will never forget. (negative: nu + o să)

In writing and in formal style, the future with “voi” + infinitive is used: “voi merge, vei merge, va merge, vom merge, veți merge, vor merge”. You’ve already seen it in the weather forecast: “va ploua” (it will rain).
For the near future, the present is enough: “Mâine merg la birou.” (I’m going to the office tomorrow.)
Congratulations! You have reached the end of level A1. Here are the main structures you now know:

Tomorrow I’m going to go to the pharmacy.
What do you say to a sick friend?
The emergency number in Romania is:
I don’t feel well. I have a temperature.
Nora has to drink tea with honey and lemon.
Nora has been ill for three days. And for three days I have been a nurse. I don’t have a diploma, but I have experience: I’ve sat next to Mrs Pop through all her colds for the last eight years.
The first rule of a good nurse: never leave the patient. So I sleep on Nora’s blanket, at her feet. It’s warm there. It’s a very good rule.
The second rule: purr. Mrs Pop says cats’ purring heals bones. I don’t know if it’s true, but Nora smiles when I purr. And a patient who smiles is a patient who is getting better.

Mrs Pop is a kind of nurse too. Three times a day she comes into the room with a tray: lime-blossom tea with honey, chicken soup, toast. Once she even brought a jar of blueberry jam, “for the vitamins”.
“You’ll get better soon,” she says every time. “But don’t rush. The body knows what it’s doing.”
On Thursday afternoon someone rings the doorbell. Mrs Pop opens the door and talks quietly with someone in the hall. Then she knocks on the bedroom door.
“Nora, you have a visitor. Are you well enough to see someone?”
Nora sits up quickly in bed and smooths her hair with her hand. “Who is it?”
The door opens and Radu comes in. He has a red nose, a hoarse voice and he is wearing… Nora’s red scarf. In his hand he has a bag from the pharmacy and a white rose.
“I came to give you back your scarf,” he says. “But Mum says I mustn’t go out without it yet. So… can I keep it until next week?”
Nora laughs, then coughs, then laughs again. “You can keep it. It’s a present.”

Radu sits on the chair next to the bed, at a distance, “so I don’t make you ill again”. He puts the rose in a glass of water on the green shelf. Then he takes two bottles of syrup out of the bag. “One for you, one for me. So we get better at the same time.”

They talk for an hour. About Enescu, about the old buildings of Cluj, about Sweden and about what they will do at Christmas. I listen to everything from the blanket, with my eyes closed. A good nurse hears everything.
When Radu leaves, Mrs Pop comes in to take the tray. She looks at the white rose on the shelf and says nothing. But I hear her singing that old song in the kitchen.
I stretch out along the whole length of the bed. My patient is smiling. My mission is over. Now I need some rest too. Nurses get tired too, you know.
nurse (a person who looks after the sick)
“o să te faci bine” = you will get better
to receive: tu primești (you receive a guest)
to arrange: ea își aranjează (she smooths, tidies)
“să ies” = the form of “a ieși” after “să”
to keep: “să-l țin” = to keep it
“să te îmbolnăvesc” = to make you ill
to take out: el scoate (he takes out)
“să ne vindecăm” = so we get better
